questions.question_text:
Two sisters share some marbles in the ratio $5:3$.
The older sister gets $14$ more marbles than the younger.
How many marbles does each sister get?

options.why: Used $14$ as the value of one part instead of the value of the $2$-part gap.
Divided $14$ by the $8$ total parts, treating $14$ as the total rather than the difference.
Added the difference of $14$ to the larger share instead of subtracting it from it.

questions.solution_text:
$5-3=2\text{ parts}$
$2\text{ parts}=14$
$1\text{ part}=7$
$5\text{ parts}=35$
$3\text{ parts}=21$
They get $35$ marbles and $21$ marbles.

questions.question_text:
Three cousins share some money in the ratio $3:5:9$.
The eldest receives $\$72$ more than the youngest.
How much does the middle cousin receive?

options.why: Used the $4$-part gap between the eldest and middle shares to find the value of one part.
Found the eldest cousin's share of $9$ parts instead of the middle cousin's share.
Found the $3$-part gap between the middle and youngest shares instead of the middle share.

questions.solution_text:
$9-3=6\text{ parts}$
$6\text{ parts}=\$72$
$1\text{ part}=\$12$
$5\text{ parts}=\$60$
The middle cousin receives $\$60$.

questions.question_text:
A rectangle has its length and width in the ratio $5:2$.
The length is $18$ cm more than the width.
Find the perimeter of the rectangle.

options.why: Added the length and the width but did not double to find the perimeter.
Used $18$ cm as the width instead of $12$ cm, reusing the stated difference as a side length.
Doubled the length only and left the two widths out of the perimeter.

questions.solution_text:
$5-2=3\text{ parts}$
$3\text{ parts}=18\text{ cm}$
$1\text{ part}=6\text{ cm}$
$5\text{ parts}=30\text{ cm}$
$2\text{ parts}=12\text{ cm}$
$P=2\times(30+12)$
$=84\text{ cm}$

questions.question_text:
In a car park the ratio of cars to vans is $9:2$.
There are $63$ more cars than vans.
How many vans are there?

options.why: Found the number of cars, $9$ parts, instead of the number of vans.
Stopped at the value of one part instead of multiplying by the vans' $2$ parts.
Divided $63$ by $9$ rather than by the $7$-part gap, then took $2$ parts.

questions.solution_text:
$9-2=7\text{ parts}$
$7\text{ parts}=63$
$1\text{ part}=9$
$2\text{ parts}=18$
There are $18$ vans.

questions.question_text:
Two sisters have savings in the ratio $7:3$.
They each spend $\$40$, and after that one sister has $\$60$ more savings than the other.
How much did the two sisters have saved altogether to begin with?

options.why: Added the $\$80$ spent back onto the total, treating the spending as having widened the gap.
Treated the $\$60$ gap as the value of one part instead of the value of $4$ parts, then multiplied by the $10$ total parts.
Treated the stated $\$60$ gap as the whole amount saved rather than as the value of $4$ parts.

questions.solution_text:
Both sisters spend the same amount, so the gap between them is unchanged.
$7-3=4\text{ parts}$
$4\text{ parts}=\$60$
$1\text{ part}=\$15$
$10\text{ parts}=\$150$

questions.question_text:
Beth and Caroline share their stickers in the ratio $1:3$.
Beth has 60 less than Caroline.
How many stickers does Caroline have?

options.why: Treats the total of four ratio parts as though it were Caroline’s share.
Multiplies the three parts by 60 instead of first finding the value of one part.
Uses only one and a half ratio parts rather than Caroline’s three parts.

questions.solution_text: The difference between the shares is $3-1=2$ parts, and these 2 parts equal 60. One part is 30, so Caroline’s 3 parts equal $3\times30=90$.

questions.question_text:
Tegwen has the same number of brothers as she has sisters.
Each one of her brothers has 50% more sisters than brothers.
How many children are in Tegwen's family?

options.why: This counts only one sibling group rather than the whole family.
This does not satisfy both sibling-number conditions.
The brother and sister counts give a larger family.

questions.solution_text:
Let Tegwen have $b$ brothers and $b$ sisters.
Each brother has $b+1$ sisters, including Tegwen, and $b-1$ brothers.
$b+1 = 1.5(b-1)$
$b = 5$
The family has $5+5+1 = 11$ children.
